title: Hierarchical data
summary: Turn Larkhaven Bikes' live station feed, JSON with lists inside lists, into tidy tables: look inside a list with str(), $, [[ and View(), keep the stations in a list-column, then spread their fields into columns and their vehicle counts into rows, and pull out just the fields you need.

steps.title: Setup: library(tidyverse), library(jsonlite)

runs.purpose: load the tidyverse, which includes tidyr

steps.explain: jsonlite reads JSON, the text format web services use to send data. tidyr has the functions that turn its nested lists into tables.

steps.title: JSON into a list: read_json() and str()

runs.purpose: read the station status feed into a list, `status`
show the list's structure, two levels deep
runs.task: Show the structure of `status`, two levels deep, with `str(status, max.level = 2)`.

steps.explain: A JSON object becomes a named list, and a JSON array an unnamed one, so `status` is lists inside lists. `str()` shows the structure: four items at the top, among them `last_updated` and `data`, and inside `data` a list of `stations`. `max.level = 2` stops `str()` from printing every station's every field, which would run to hundreds of lines.

steps.title: Inside a list: $, [[ and View()

runs.task: Show the first station in the feed: `status$data$stations`, then its first item with `[[1]]`.

runs.purpose: open the list in RStudio's viewer, to explore it by clicking

steps.explain: `$` takes an item from a list by name, and `[[1]]` the first item by position; chained, they walk down the levels. Station {first_id} had {first_bikes} bikes available when the feed was made. `[[` returns the item itself, while `[` would return a smaller list holding it. `View()` opens a list in a Source tab where you can expand each level by clicking, and its button at the end of each row writes the code that reaches that item.

steps.title: A list-column: one row per station

runs.purpose: put the stations in a tibble, each station's list in one cell, as `stations`
runs.task: Make a tibble with one column, `station`, holding `status$data$stations`, and store it in `stations`.

steps.explain: A tibble's column can be a list: a list-column. `stations` has {n_stations} rows, one per station, and each cell holds that station's whole list of fields, which the printout summarises as `<named list [8]>` or `[9]`. One row per station is the right shape already; the fields still have to come out of the cells.

steps.title: Fields into columns: unnest_wider()

runs.purpose: spread each station's fields into columns
runs.task: Spread the fields in `station` into columns with `unnest_wider()`.

steps.explain: `unnest_wider()` makes a column of each named field. Most fields hold one value, so they become ordinary columns, typed as numbers, text and `TRUE`/`FALSE`. A field only some stations have, `num_docks_disabled`, is `NA` for the others: only {n_disabled} report it. `vehicle_types_available` is still a list-column, because each of its cells holds a list of vehicle types.

steps.title: Lists into rows: unnest_longer()

alternatives: stations |> unnest_wider(station) |> unnest_longer(vehicle_types_available) |> unnest_wider(vehicle_types_available, names_sep = NULL)
runs.purpose: give each station one row per vehicle type, with the type and its count as columns
runs.task: After `unnest_wider(station)`, give each vehicle type its own row with `unnest_longer(vehicle_types_available)`, then spread its fields with `unnest_wider(vehicle_types_available)`.

steps.explain: `unnest_longer()` turns each element of a list into a row of its own, repeating the station's other columns. Stations with both classic bikes and e-bikes get two rows and the rest one: {n_rows} rows in all. Each element is itself a little list, a type and a count, so `unnest_wider()` spreads it into `vehicle_type_id` and `count`. Nested data comes apart one level at a time: wider for named fields, longer for unnamed lists.

steps.title: Pull out what you need: hoist()

runs.purpose: read the station information feed into `info`

alternatives: tibble(station = info$data$stations) |> hoist(station, station_id = 'station_id', name = list('name', 1, 'text'), capacity = 'capacity')
runs.purpose: pull each station's ID, its name in the first language, and its capacity out of the lists
runs.task: Put `info$data$stations` in a tibble's `station` column, then pull out `"station_id"`, `"capacity"` and `name`: the `"text"` of the `"name"` field's first item, `list("name", 1, "text")`, with `hoist()`.

steps.explain: In this feed a station's name is a list of translations, each with a `text` and a `language`, as in the GBFS standard that real bike-share schemes publish. `hoist()` reaches into each cell and pulls out just the fields named, at any depth: `list("name", 1, "text")` means the name field, its first item, its text, such as "{first_name}". Everything not pulled out stays behind in `station`, a smaller list, so nothing is lost.
